content: Lithium nitride is a chemical compound composed of lithium and nitrogen, with the molecular formula Li₃N. It is the only stable nitride of an alkali metal. This compound appears as a solid with a red or purple coloration, possesses a high melting point, and exhibits ionic properties. Its crystal structure is unique, consisting of two distinct types of layers: one layer with the composition Li₂N, which contains lithium ions coordinated in a six-fold manner, and another layer composed solely of lithium ions. Lithium nitride is recognized as a fast ion conductor and demonstrates the highest ionic conductivity among all inorganic lithium salts. It can be synthesized through the direct reaction of lithium and nitrogen. This can be achieved either by burning lithium metal in pure nitrogen gas or by reacting nitrogen gas with lithium dissolved in liquid sodium metal. The latter method yields a purer product. When lithium nitride reacts with water, it undergoes a vigorous reaction to produce ammonia, as represented by the equation: Li₃N (s) + 3 H₂O (l) → 3 LiOH (aq) + NH₃ (g). This behavior is characteristic of all ionic nitrides due to the N³⁻ ion, which is an exceptionally strong Brønsted base. The nitride ion qualifies as a superbasic species and is even a stronger base than the hydride ion. Consequently, it can deprotonate molecular hydrogen, as shown in the reaction: Li₃N (s) + 2 H₂ (g) → LiNH₂ (s) + 2 LiH (s). Lithium nitride is currently being explored as a potential medium for hydrogen gas storage. This is because the reaction involving hydrogen absorption and release is reversible at a temperature of 270°C. A hydrogen absorption capacity of 5% by weight has been achieved in experimental studies.
